segments: The Book of the Generations of Nations. {OCR?}
to him, the Turks:
"Sell to us."
And when they gave him their word,
he sent, brought gold, and paid,
and redeemed the captives.
Now they were fifteen thousand.
These small things, indeed, we have written,
so that it might be known how powerful our people once were,
and to what misery their descendants have handed down {OCR?}.
And in this year, the Emir Abu Nasr was seized,
and the Emir and commander of the army, Baha al-Dawlah, took his place.
When this man became powerful,
he coveted the possessions of the Caliph al-Ta'i',
and made a conspiracy with the Daylamites.
And one of the days,
while al-Ta'i' was sitting upon his throne,
they overturned him and wrapped him in the carpet that was under him,
and imprisoned him,
and took his abdication in his own handwriting.
And they brought Abu'l-Abbas Ahmad, son of Ishaq, son of al-Muqtadir,
and made him king in the year 381,
381 of the Arabs,
and gave him the cognomen al-Qadir.
After al-Ta'i', al-Qadir [ruled for] forty-one years and three months.
In the year 382,
382 of the Arabs,
which is the year 1304,
1304 of the Greeks,
(993 of our Lord):
The Romans became masters over Khilat, and Manzikert, and Arjish.
Then Abu Ali, the general of the Armenians, took upon himself to give tribute to the Romans.
And King Basil agreed, and left Armenia in his hands,
and made a peace for ten years.
At this time, a great multitude of Armenians departed who were called the Senekerimites, that is, of the race of Sennacherib,
and they surrendered their fortresses to King Basil of the Romans.
And he, in return for them, gave them Sebastia of Cappadocia,
and patricians were appointed in it from among the Armenians.
And from there they spread throughout all Cappadocia, Cilicia, and Syria.
It is said
that Adrammelech and Sharezer,
when they killed Sennacherib their father,
fled to the mountains of Qardu,
and mingled with the Armenians.
And from here the Armenians acquired this surname,
so as to be called Sennacheribites.
At this time, when Sa'd al-Dawlah, the Emir of Aleppo, fell sick and died,
he commanded that his son Abu'l-Fada'il should take his place,
and that Lu'lu', the commander of the army, should be his governor.
Then al-Aziz, the Caliph of Egypt,
his soul desired to rule over Aleppo,
and to gain control over its treasures.
And he sent Mangutakin, his slave, with thirty thousand horsemen against Aleppo.
